messages.content: A neural network is a computational model inspired by the human brain. It consists of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons) that process inputs, learn patterns through weighted connections, and make predictions.
Can you give me a simple real-life analogy for it?

Think of a neural network like an assembly line of factory workers making a decision: each worker (neuron) inspects one specific detail, adjusts their confidence, and passes the signal forward until the final supervisor makes the ultimate decision.
How does it differ from a decision tree?

Unlike a neural network which combines continuous numerical weights across layers, a decision tree makes discrete, rule-based binary splits (IF-THEN conditions). Decision trees are transparent and easy to interpret, whereas neural networks excel at high-dimensional unstructured data.
Going back to your analogy -- how would a decision tree use it differently?

In our factory analogy, instead of all workers whispering and collectively adjusting continuous weights, a decision tree works like a single inspector following a strict sequential flowchart: first checking condition A (e.g. part size > 10cm), then branching to condition B, until reaching a definitive decision.
